edges.effect_quant: Across pooled cohort studies, highest-versus-lowest coffee intake is usually close to null, although one dose-response review reported a small per-cup increase in pancreatic-cancer risk.
edges.mechanism: Coffee changes glucose handling, bile-acid exposure, and several xenobiotic-metabolism pathways, so both beneficial and adverse pancreatic hypotheses have been proposed. In practice, the epidemiology looks more vulnerable to residual confounding and exposure misclassification than to one clean biologic story.
edges.summary: This is not a convincing cancer-prevention edge in either direction. The strongest pooled cohort analyses cluster around no clear association, while one dose-response meta-analysis suggested a small increase per extra cup per day, so the safest read is contested evidence with no actionable conclusion.
edges.caveats: Smoking, reverse causation from preclinical digestive symptoms, and broad differences in brewing method make this literature hard to interpret cleanly. A weak signal in one dose-response model should not be overread as proof that coffee causes pancreatic cancer.
